review_schema.title: Blind review of one method clone
review_schema.description: A reviewer agent with a blind id scores src/ and test/ from git diff refs/tags/starter..HEAD. Every score runs from 1, worst, to 5, best, with a reason of one or two sentences.

alterability.title: Alterability
alterability.description: How little code each change case of docs/SPEC.md touches, given that all combinations of both must work.

test_quality.title: Test quality
test_quality.description: How well the method's own tests in test/ pin the rules and variants of the spec, with clear names and independent cases.

pipeline.notation: Once means one agent runs the steps. Repeat per unit means one agent per unit until no unit is open. Throughout means the rule joins every prompt. For up to n starts means separate attempts with the best kept. The harness does means the harness runs the step without an agent. If names the event that starts a stage, and with adds a rule borrowed from another method. Steps are quoted from args.json with their numbers. Tag: verified.
pipeline.weight_text: Weighted tokens count input 1, cache creation 1.25, cache read 0.05 and output 5 per token. These are claude-opus-5-5 prices relative to an input token and state no dollar cost.

awards.title: Best overall
awards.rule: Lowest plain sum of each method's ranks on M, E and alignment, ties sharing their average rank. Cheapest and consistency never count.

awards.title: Most cost effective
awards.rule: Lowest M, the cost to completion times 1 minus APFDc-H, among methods with a functional mark of 15/15. M_io leaves output tokens out.

awards.title: Fewest errors

awards.title: Best CQP/PMD alignment

awards.title: Cheapest

functions.name: agrees

functions.name: aligned

functions.name: places
functions.doc: Competition places, lower first, ties sharing the best place.

functions.name: podium

functions.name: overall

functions.name: award

functions.name: awards
functions.doc: The award list. spread is {scores: {name: C}, p, runs, n: {name: builds}, builds, drift: [{name, x, y, p}]} of the replicates pooled over the joined contrasts runs, None without one.

stats.name: wilson
stats.doc: (lo, hi) Wilson score interval of k successes in n trials, which stays inside 0 to 1 at k = 0 and k = n.

stats.name: fisher_exact
stats.doc: Two-sided Fisher exact p of the 2x2 table [[a, b], [c, d]]: the summed probability of every table with the same margins that is no more likely than this one. Integer weights keep ties exact.

stats.name: holm
stats.doc: Holm step-down adjusted p values in the order of ps, each capped at 1 and none below a smaller p's.

stats.name: fisher_pairs
stats.doc: {(i, j): (p, Holm p)} of the Fisher exact test of each pair of rows i < j of a k x 2 table, Holm-adjusted over every pair.

stats.name: chi2_rows
stats.doc: Pearson chi-square of a k x 2 table from each row's successes and size, 0 when a column is empty. An empty row adds nothing.

stats.name: permutation_chi2
stats.doc: (chi-square, p) of the k x 2 table of (successes, failures) rows. p is the share of seeded label shuffles, counting the observed one, whose chi-square reaches the observed.

stats.name: deviations
stats.doc: Each value's absolute deviation from its group median.

stats.name: brown_forsythe
stats.doc: Brown-Forsythe F: one-way ANOVA F of each value's absolute deviation from its group median.

stats.name: anova_f
stats.doc: One-way ANOVA F. inf when the values vary between groups only, 0 when they do not vary at all.

stats.name: brown_forsythe_permutation
stats.doc: (F, p) of brown_forsythe. p is the share of seeded shuffles of the pooled deviations from each value's own group median over groups of the same sizes, counting the observed one, whose F reaches the observed. Shuffling raw values would mix the group medians into the spread.

stats.name: ranks
stats.doc: 1-based ranks with ties given their average rank.

stats.name: mann_whitney_exact
stats.doc: (U, p) of the exact two-sided Mann-Whitney test. U counts the pairs with x above y, ties as half. p is the share of every split of the pooled average ranks into a group of len(xs) whose rank sum lies at least as far from its mean as the observed, so ties stay exact. The C(n, len(xs)) splits suit small samples only.

stats.name: weighted_kappa
stats.doc: Cohen's linearly weighted kappa of two raters' numeric ratings of the same items: 1 minus the mean |x - y| over its chance mean across every pairing of the two raters' ratings. None when chance disagreement is 0.

stats.name: jaccard
stats.doc: Shared items over all items of two collections. Two empty ones agree fully and give 1.

stats.name: spearman
stats.doc: Spearman rho as Pearson r of average ranks, None when either side has no spread.

stats.name: spearman_trial
stats.doc: (rho, p, lo, hi, skipped): p is the share of seeded shuffles of ys, counting the observed one, whose |rho| reaches the observed, against the null rho = 0. lo to hi is the seeded percentile bootstrap 95% interval over resampled pairs, skipping the resamples with no spread, which skipped counts. lo and hi are None when no resample has spread. All None when either side has no spread.

methodologies.title: TDD-adjacent methodologies
methodologies.text: This page lays out development methods from a forum post on TDD as greedy pathing so they can be trialled on a new repo. Classic TDD behaves like greedy local search and each variant changes one part of that search. That part is the map, the step size, the breadth or the check.

methodologies.title: Summary
methodologies.text:
| Method | Family | What it changes in the search | Idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classic greedy TDD | Baseline | Nothing. It is the greedy baseline. | Smallest failing test then smallest passing change. |
| Noun-verb map | Structure first | The map. Fixed before any code. | Plan classes from spec nouns and methods from verbs. Fill linked stubs. |
| Mapped-path TDD | Structure first | The map. Tests follow a planned route on it. | Walk the map leaves first toward one acceptance test at a time. |
| Functions first, classes later | Structure first | The map. Drawn after the code exists. | Test-drive pure functions. Cluster them into classes later. |
| Transformation Priority Premise TDD | Step size | Move order. Cheapest transformation first. | Pick tests the simplest ranked transformation can pass. |
| Coarse-to-fine TDD | Step size | Step size. Large first then shrink on a stall. | One big step per feature. Drop a gear when it stalls. |
| Annealed refactoring | Step size | Accepts worse designs early then cools. | Uphill refactors allowed early on a fixed cooling schedule. |
| Multi-start TDD | Search and validation | Breadth. Several starts and the best is kept. | Independent attempts on one locked suite. Score rule fixed first. |
| Most informative next test | Search and validation | The check. Next test kills surviving mutants. | Write the test that rules out the most wrong implementations. |
| Property-based TDD | Search and validation | The check. One test covers an input region. | State rules over input regions. Generators sample and shrink. |
| Held-out TDD | Search and validation | The check. Hidden tests score milestones. | Visible tests drive the loop. Hidden tests measure overfitting. |
| Anchor Engineering | Search and validation | The check. Anchors and their criteria gate each milestone. | Write claims that must hold with their checks. Build milestones behind a mutation gate and a judge. |
| tcp-untreated | Test-list order | Test order. The list as the lister wrote it. | Control. Build the shared list in its written order. |
| tcp-random | Test-list order | Test order. One seeded shuffle. | Control. Build the shared list in a logged random order. |
| tcp-coverage | Test-list order | Test order. Most new clauses first. | Rank candidates by clauses no earlier candidate checks. |
| tcp-cost | Test-list order | Test order. Least cost per new clause first. | Rank candidates by estimated lines per new clause. |
| tcp-risk | Test-list order | Test order. Riskiest clauses first. | Rank candidates by the mean risk of the clauses they check. |
| tcp-usage | Test-list order | Test order. Most used clauses first. | Rank candidates by the usage share no earlier candidate checks. |

methodologies.title: Classic greedy TDD
methodologies.text:
Grow the code one smallest failing test at a time. Make the smallest passing change and tidy on green.

**Mirrors:** greedy local search. Only improving moves are accepted as in annealing at zero temperature.

1. List test scenarios from the requirements before writing code.
2. Pick the scenario that needs the least new code.
3. Write one failing test for it and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Reject assistant diffs that do more.
5. Fake a constant if unsure. Generalize once a second example forces it.
6. Type the obvious code when sure. Drop back to faking on a surprise red.
7. Refactor on green. Add new scenarios to the list. Repeat until empty.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** each map verb seeds at least one scenario. Leaf nouns such as Seed and House go before Board and Game.

**Measure:** red-green cycles per feature. Impasses where a bar stays red over 15 minutes. Lines changed per green commit.

**Fits when:** requirements are clear and small worked examples exist. It is the baseline for every other method.

**Risk:** small steps can settle into a local design that later needs a rewrite. Code can overfit the visible tests and test order changes the result. Assistants resist tiny steps. The A02 notes record the assistant doing everything at once despite rewording.

methodologies.title: Structure first
methodologies.text: Noun-verb from COMPSCI 701 A02 is the reference example. The other two reuse or invert its map.

methodologies.title: Noun-verb map (adapted from COMPSCI 701 A02)
methodologies.text:
Plan classes from the spec's nouns and methods from its verbs before any code. Then fill the plan one linked stub at a time.

**Mirrors:** fixing a network architecture before training the weights. The map bounds the search space.

1. Gather the spec and its acceptance tests. Write tests for any untested feature.
2. Extract every noun and verb as Noun: -verb lists. Trim to the domain.
3. Mark parents as Noun(Parent). Split nouns over 4 verbs. Apply Clean Code names.
4. Replace duplicate verbs with references written as verb1(Noun2.verb3).
5. Script-check for cycles, dangling references and nouns over 4 verbs. Fix each.
6. Scaffold stubs that throw a TODO naming the referenced method. Fill one per prompt.
7. Run the tests. Fix one failing test per prompt with the smallest change.
8. Lint with no suppressions. Prune unused methods. Diff a regenerated map against the plan.

Part of the A02 map from `kalah_nouns_verbs.txt`:

```
Game(Kalah):
- play(Board.initialise)
- start(Board.initialise)
- finish(Turn.isFinished)
- score(Player.collectSeeds)

Board(Game):
- initialise(Player.chooseHouse)
- sow(House.addSeed)
- wrap(Move.distribute)
- placeSeed(House.addSeed)
- isOwnedBy(Player.ownsHouse)

Turn(Game):
- chooseHouse(Player.chooseHouse)
- execute(Move.distribute)
- nextPlayer(Player.hasMoves)
- isFinished(Game.finish)
```

Step 5 would flag two defects here. Game.finish and Turn.isFinished call each other. Board has 5 verbs.

**What A02 taught:** linked TODO stubs kept the assistant on the plan after a whole-program first attempt failed. Test fixing took 187.8 of 264.7 credits (71 percent). Filling every TODO before the first test run is the likely cause.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** it is the map. Steps 2 to 5 are the planning stage the other methods reuse.

**Measure:** credits per step. Map defects caught at step 5. Plan drift at step 8. Suppressions or build-file edits the assistant attempts.

**Fits when:** a spec or rubric names the domain objects and actions. The domain fits one map of about 10 nouns.

**Risk:** the A02 plan carried 5 two-way cycles and 1 dangling reference that no step checked. The assistant also suppressed PMD warnings and edited the Makefile until told not to. Untested additions to the A02 run are the test writing in step 1, the script check in step 5, the one-per-prompt limits in steps 6 and 7 and the plan diff in step 8.

methodologies.title: Mapped-path TDD
methodologies.text:
Treat the checked map as a fixed graph. Order tests along a route from leaf verbs up to one acceptance test at a time.

**Mirrors:** planning on a fixed graph. A leaves-first topological walk gives the route and the remaining verbs give an A*-style distance estimate.

1. Build and check the map using steps 2 to 5 of noun-verb.
2. Read each verb1(Noun2.verb3) reference as a call edge between verbs.
3. Write one failing end-to-end acceptance test for the next spec feature.
4. List the verbs that test reaches. Order them leaves first.
5. Per verb write the smallest failing unit test then the smallest passing change.
6. Run all tests and lint after each verb. Refactor only while green.
7. Add any verb the route lacks to the map first. Then re-route.
8. Repeat from step 3 until every feature passes. Then diff the map.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** the map is the search graph. Each unit test walks one verb on the route.

**Measure:** credits per verb against the A02 test-fix share of 71 percent. Prompts per verb from red to green. Route replans and map edits.

**Fits when:** each feature has an end-to-end acceptance test such as the Kalah input and output specifications. The call graph is shallow. The route caps an assistant that jumps ahead at one verb per prompt.

**Risk:** a wrong map gives a wrong route and may build verbs the acceptance test never needs. End-to-end feedback comes late. A cycle the map check missed blocks any topological order.

methodologies.title: Functions first, classes later
methodologies.text:
Test-drive pure functions over plain data. Group them into classes later by the data they touch and who calls them.

**Mirrors:** search-based module clustering as in Bunch. Step 6 is a greedy one-pass version of that search.

1. List the spec's verbs as a test backlog. Leave nouns for later.
2. Model state as plain data records with no behaviour.
3. Test-drive each verb as a pure function over that data.
4. Keep input and output in one thin shell that calls the pure functions.
5. Tabulate each function's callees and the record fields it reads or writes.
6. Assign each function to the record it touches most. Else join its main caller.
7. Split any cluster over the lint method cap. Move each into a noun-named class.
8. Keep tests green. Regenerate the noun-verb map. Count cross-cluster calls. Lint.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** it runs the map in reverse. Verbs come first and nouns emerge as clusters.

**Measure:** tests that need test doubles, aiming near zero. Calls inside clusters against calls across them. Test edits forced by the move into classes.

**Fits when:** domain logic is heavy and input and output are thin as in a board game engine. The right objects are unclear from the spec.

**Risk:** a Java ruleset like A02's fails lint before clustering. Records trip DataClass and one function holder trips TooManyMethods at 10. The records are an early noun decision in disguise. The step 6 rule is greedy and depends on how records were drawn.

methodologies.title: Transformation Priority Premise TDD
methodologies.text:
Pick each next test so the simplest transformation on Martin's ranked list passes it. Back up when only a costly one would. Accept it when no simpler test exists.

**Mirrors:** depth-first backtracking search with cheapest-first move ordering.

Martin's list from highest to lowest rank is `{}->nil`, constant, constant+, scalar, statements, if, array, container, recursion, while, function and `variable->assignment`.

1. Put Martin's ranked list with one-line definitions in the assistant prompt.
2. Pick the next test that the highest-ranked transformation can pass.
3. Pass it with that one transformation. Name it in the commit message.
4. Revert and try a simpler test if it needs while, function or assignment.
5. Accept the lower-ranked move and log it if no simpler test exists.
6. Refactor on green. Refactors change structure and never behaviour.
7. Repeat until the test list is empty.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** the map fixes nouns and verb signatures. TPP grows each verb body from nil upward. A reach for container or function flags a missing noun.

**Measure:** transformation rank per green commit. Backtracks to a simpler test. Impasses per feature.

**Fits when:** pure algorithmic cores such as Kalah sowing and capture rules keep causing impasses in classic TDD.

**Risk:** TPP is an unproven premise backed by one sorting kata. Labelling every move costs time. A lean toward recursion can hit stack limits in Java.

methodologies.title: Coarse-to-fine TDD
methodologies.text:
Start each feature with one big step against an acceptance test. Shrink the step by a fixed rule when progress stalls.

**Mirrors:** a learning rate that decays on a plateau as in Keras ReduceLROnPlateau and restarts high per feature as in SGDR.

1. Write one failing end-to-end acceptance test for the next feature.
2. Set four gears: feature, class, method, fake-it. Start in the feature gear.
3. Attempt the whole feature in one assistant prompt against the acceptance test.
4. Shrink rule: one failed attempt or 10 minutes red. Revert and drop a gear.
5. In lower gears drive each class or method with its own unit test.
6. Fake-it gear is classic TDD. Split any test still stuck there.
7. Once acceptance passes add edge-case unit tests. Refactor on green.
8. Return to the feature gear for the next feature.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** the root noun anchors the acceptance test. Each gear down walks one level of the noun hierarchy.

**Measure:** minutes to first green acceptance test. Gear drops per feature. Lines discarded per revert. Mutation score on feature-gear code.

**Fits when:** the repo has a clear end-to-end entry point such as a CLI or game loop. An assistant can write a large first draft fast.

**Risk:** a big early step can lock in a poor structure. Big-step code may stay thinly tested until the edge-case pass. The thresholds have no source and need tuning per repo.

methodologies.title: Annealed refactoring
methodologies.text:
Run classic TDD. After each green allow refactors that briefly worsen the design to escape a poor structure. Tighten the allowance on a fixed schedule until only non-worsening moves remain.

**Mirrors:** threshold accepting. This deterministic variant of simulated annealing accepts any move worse by less than a falling threshold.

1. Run classic TDD. Log energy per commit: PMD warnings plus jdeps class edges.
2. Hot may move nouns and verbs. Warm moves verbs. Cold renames and extracts.
3. Timebox and allowed rise: hot 45 min 20%. Warm 15 min 5%. Cold 5 min 0%.
4. After each green try at most one allowed move on a throwaway branch.
5. Pick the move after which the next test needs the fewest changed lines to pass.
6. Merge if energy does not rise. Merge a rise within budget with a one-line reason.
7. Revert any move still red or over budget when its timebox ends.
8. Cool one phase per third of the original test list. Stay cold after.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** hot phases may redraw the map. Cold phases freeze it.

**Measure:** energy per commit. Uphill moves tried, kept and reverted. Final energy against the classic baseline.

**Fits when:** the first map is a guess and class boundaries look wrong. Greedy refactoring has stalled. The repo is Java or has an equivalent warning and dependency counter.

**Risk:** annealing over refactoring moves has been reported to give incoherent designs. The metric is a proxy and can be gamed. Rises can add up so track the best energy seen.

methodologies.title: Multi-start TDD
methodologies.text:
Run several independent attempts against one locked acceptance suite. Keep the best by a rule fixed before any attempt starts.

**Mirrors:** random-restart hill climbing. Set-based design likewise narrows several live options over time.

1. Write the shared acceptance tests and lock them with a hash check in CI.
2. Fix budget and score up front. Default is green first then mutation score then fewer lines.
3. Pick 2 to 4 start strategies such as noun-verb map, smallest-test TDD or functions first.
4. Run each attempt on its own branch until green or out of budget.
5. At half budget drop any attempt passing under half the leader's tests.
6. Score the finished attempts. If none is green rank by tests passed.
7. Keep the winner. Archive the others with a note on what each taught.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** give each attempt a map with a different split rule such as above 4 verbs or above 6.

**Measure:** credits and time to first green per attempt. Edits to locked tests, expected zero. Spread between best and worst score.

**Fits when:** the class layout of a new repo is still open and two or more designs look plausible.

**Risk:** cost grows with each attempt and each repeats the costly test-fix phase. A score chosen after seeing results is cherry-picking. The A02 comparison came after both branches existed. Attempts from one model share blind spots.

methodologies.title: Most informative next test (mutation-guided TDD)
methodologies.text:
After each requirement goes green write the test that rules out the most wrong implementations still passing. Surviving mutants stand in for them.

**Mirrors:** query by committee. Surviving mutants are a local committee and each killing test shrinks the version space.

1. Finish one requirement with red-green-refactor cycles as usual.
2. Run PIT or mutmut on the code that requirement touched.
3. List surviving mutants. Set aside those no input could tell apart.
4. Keep survivors that change an output a requirement names.
5. Write the smallest requirement-level test that kills the most kept survivors.
6. Take expected values from the requirement. Never from the current code's output.
7. If the test fails on real code treat it as red and fix the code.
8. Rerun mutation until no kept survivor remains. Then take the next requirement.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** run mutation per noun. Every verb needs at least one killing test.

**Measure:** mutation score per class per requirement. Real defects found by killing tests. Tests that broke in later refactors.

**Fits when:** logic-heavy code has a fast unit suite. Java has PIT and Python has mutmut.

**Risk:** mutation runs are slow so scope them to touched code. Equivalent mutants waste time. Chasing a perfect score pins implementation detail. An AI may copy current output as the expected value.

methodologies.title: Property-based TDD
methodologies.text:
Each test states a rule over a region of inputs. A generator samples the region and shrinks any failure to a small case.

**Mirrors:** each run is a fresh random minibatch. Widening the generator is a curriculum. Shrinking is a local search for the smallest failing input.

1. Phrase the next requirement as an invariant, round trip or model comparison.
2. Write a generator for a narrow slice of valid inputs.
3. Run the property and watch it fail with a shrunk counterexample.
4. Make the smallest change that makes the property pass.
5. Widen the generator toward all valid inputs and repeat until green.
6. Save each shrunk counterexample as a fixed example test.
7. Refactor with the properties as the safety net.
8. In CI log the seed and replay saved failures before fresh random cases.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** one invariant per noun such as a seed total that never changes. One contract property per verb.

**Measure:** properties per verb. Defects caught that example tests missed. Failures that do not replay from their seed.

**Fits when:** rules state as invariants or round trips and the input space is large. Java has jqwik and Python has Hypothesis.

**Risk:** UI and IO glue have no clear property. Weak properties pass trivially and narrow generators give false comfort. Random runs look flaky unless seeds are logged.

methodologies.title: Held-out TDD
methodologies.text:
Visible tests drive the red-green loop. Hidden tests that the implementer never sees score milestones.

**Mirrors:** a train and validation split. The gap between visible and hidden pass rates measures overfitting.

1. Pin the public interface first such as the CLI or the noun-verb verbs.
2. A human or separate agent writes several black-box cases per requirement.
3. Move about a third of each requirement's cases into a hidden set.
4. Keep hidden tests in a private repo that only CI checks out. Keep its CI token out of the agent environment.
5. Clone it outside the agent workspace. Add a permissions deny entry for that path in the assistant settings.
6. Drive TDD and AI loops with the visible set alone.
7. On each merge CI prints hidden pass counts per requirement. Log the gap.
8. On a hidden failure write a fresh visible test. Replace that hidden case.

**Pairs with noun-verb:** pin the map's public verbs as the interface both sets test. The gap per noun shows where the code overfits.

**Measure:** visible and hidden pass rate per merge. Gap per noun. Hidden cases replaced after disclosure.

**Fits when:** an AI loop iterates hard against tests and a human or separate agent owns the hidden set.

**Risk:** each look at the hidden score leaks a little so the set ages with reuse. A solo author has seen the hidden tests so only the AI side is held out. CI logs that print assertions leak the set.

methodologies.title: Anchor Engineering
methodologies.text:
An Anchor Book in the repository holds the design, anchors that state what must be true about the system, the criterion that verifies each anchor and the planned chunks of work. Agents build each chunk in test and fix loops behind deterministic tests, mutation testing and a judge review.

Adapted from Wilhelm 2026 Principles of Anchor Engineering. The post states principles and defers the mechanics to later posts, so the steps below are this page's construction. An unattended run has no human, so an agent judge takes the place of the human judgement check-in. The judge review is the only review. Each planned chunk of work is a milestone. The Book is ANCHORS.md at the clone root.

1. Write the Anchor Book ANCHORS.md at the clone root from README.md and docs/SPEC.md. It holds the design, each anchor as a claim that must hold about the system, the criterion that verifies it, and the planned chunks of work as milestones.
2. Check each anchor against the others and the spec. Log each conflict and the decision taken in the Book.
3. Per milestone, turn each of its anchors into tests that check it. Record in the Book which tests verify which anchor. Test names describe behaviour and carry no anchor ids.
4. Write code until those tests pass, in an agent test and fix loop.
5. Run the deterministic gate: ./run.sh test, ./run.sh lint and ./run.sh mutate. Add tests for surviving mutants that break an anchor.
6. Review the milestone as a judge for structure and correctness against its anchors. Fix what the review finds.
7. Keep the Book current as the code changes. Log each decision and mark each milestone done.

**Measure:** the mutation score at each gate, anchors with a passing test over all anchors, decisions and conflicts logged, and judge findings found and fixed.

**Fits when:** a spec already states what must hold and a fast unit suite has mutation testing.

**Risk:** the post reports no measured result. Its defining input is human judgement in the Book, and an agent-written Book has none. Anchors drawn from docs/SPEC.md may restate the spec and overlap the shared test list.

methodologies.title: Test-list order
methodologies.text:
One lister writes a shared test list from the spec before any arm runs. Every arm builds that list with the same four steps in an order the harness computes from it, so the arms differ only in the order. Classic greedy TDD and Transformation Priority Premise TDD already prescribe a cost order. Khan and Arshad find no test-list development method in the literature (p. 52), so each arm here states its rule over a fixed list.

**Mirrors:** test case prioritization for regression testing (Rothermel et al. 2001). Its untreated and random controls become tcp-untreated and tcp-random.

The rules use these terms. checks are the clauses a candidate's assertions observe and relies the clauses it needs and does not assert. The covered set K is the union of checks over the candidates already ranked. gain is the count of a candidate's checks outside K. The seeded order is TESTLIST.md shuffled once by the run seed, and every final tie goes to the earlier candidate in it.

A list-only run computes every order before any arm runs. It reports the normalized Kendall distance between each pair of orders and a cost-only order, estimate ascending as in classic. Of two orders closer than 0.15 only one arm launches, and no arm that close to the cost-only order launches. The user picks the arm that stays. The threshold was fixed before any data. The arm set then stays fixed across repeats and each repeat gets a fresh list.

Added candidates go after every initial candidate in arrival order and no arm re-ranks them.

**Risk:** clause tags, ratings and estimates are the lister's claims and no reviewer checks them. Two rules can give nearly the same order on a list of 12. The steps lack the fake-it and reject-larger-diff rules of classic, so classic is no order-only baseline and tcp-untreated and tcp-random serve as the family's baselines.

methodologies.title: Shared test list
methodologies.text:
One lister agent works once per run in its own clone and writes the list every arm shares.

1. Number each functional rule in README.md and docs/SPEC.md as a clause R1 to Rn in CLAUSES.md. Leave out code quality and PMD rules.
2. Rate each clause 1 to 3 for the chance a first implementation gets it wrong. Rate its usage 1 to 100 as the percent of moves in a typical game that exercise it. Rate a clause of one variant as the percent of games that use the variant times the share of their moves that exercise it.
3. List at most 12 candidate tests in TESTLIST.md. Each names one behaviour.
4. Give each candidate two fields. checks lists every clause its assertions observe, variants included. relies lists clauses it needs and does not assert.
5. Estimate the production lines each candidate needs on the starter alone.
6. Commit both files and return them as JSON.

The harness checks the JSON before any arm starts. Ids are unique, checks and relies name real clauses, there are 1 to 12 candidates, risk is 1 to 3, usage is 1 to 100 and each estimate is a whole number. A failed check stops the family. The harness divides each usage by the sum over all clauses, so the usage shares sum to 1.

methodologies.title: tcp-untreated (written order control)
methodologies.text:
Build the shared list in the order the lister wrote it.

**Basis:** Rothermel et al. use untreated order as a control and conjecture that it reflects how a suite was built (pp. 931-932 and 946). Against tcp-random it estimates the effect of the lister's order.

**Order:** TESTLIST.md as written.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** clauses in the checks of built candidates after each iteration. Candidates logged in ADDED.md.

methodologies.title: tcp-random (seeded order control)
methodologies.text:
Build the shared list in one random order fixed by the run seed.

**Basis:** Rothermel et al. use random order as a control (pp. 931-932). The seed is logged in args.json.

**Order:** the seeded order.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** clauses in the checks of built candidates after each iteration. Candidates logged in ADDED.md.

methodologies.title: tcp-coverage (additional clause coverage)
methodologies.text:
Build first the candidate that checks the most clauses no earlier candidate checks.

**Basis:** Rothermel M5, additional statement coverage with a reset once coverage is complete (pp. 932-933), with clauses in place of statements. Rothermel names cost per coverage of requirement features as an option (p. 931), which supports the use of clauses. It finds no clear winner between total and additional coverage (p. 946). The transfer to a TDD list is unchecked.

**Order:**

- Pick next the candidate with the largest gain.
- When every unranked candidate has gain 0, empty K and apply the rule again.
- Candidates with empty checks go last. Final ties follow the seeded order.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** clauses in the checks of built candidates after each iteration. Candidates logged in ADDED.md. Candidates whose test passed on its first run with no red.

methodologies.title: tcp-cost (cost per additional clause)
methodologies.text:
Build first the candidate with the fewest estimated lines per new clause.

**Basis:** Rothermel names ordering by increasing cost per coverage of requirement features (p. 931). It reports Wong et al. ordering by increasing cost per additional coverage after safe test selection (p. 937). The transfer to a TDD list is unchecked.

**Order:**

- Pick next the candidate with the smallest (estimate + 1) divided by gain, over candidates with gain above 0. The 1 keeps a 0-line estimate finite.
- When no unranked candidate has gain above 0, empty K and apply the rule again.
- Candidates with empty checks go last by estimate ascending. Final ties follow the seeded order.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** estimated lines against src lines added per candidate in git log. Clauses in the checks of built candidates after each iteration. Candidates logged in ADDED.md.

methodologies.title: tcp-risk (riskiest clauses first)
methodologies.text:
Build first the candidate whose clauses a first implementation most likely gets wrong.

**Basis:** Rothermel names faster detection of high-risk faults as a prioritization goal (p. 930). Mukherjee and Patnaik report risk-based prioritization studies (p. 1049). The 1 to 3 rating and the mean are design choices and unchecked.

**Order:**

- Score each candidate as the mean risk over its checks.
- Pick candidates by score, highest first.
- Candidates with empty checks go last. Final ties follow the seeded order.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** risk of each built candidate's riskiest clause against its red-green cycles in LOG.md. Candidates logged in ADDED.md.

methodologies.title: tcp-usage (most used clauses first)
methodologies.text:
Build first the candidate whose new clauses carry the most usage share.

**Basis:** Rothermel et al. report as related work that Avritzer and Weyuker order generated tests to cover more operational-profile probability mass earlier, for software modelled as a Markov chain (pp. 936-937). Rothermel gives no evaluation of it. The spec has no operational profile, so the lister's usage estimate stands in for one. The transfer to a TDD list is unchecked.

**Order:**

- A clause's share is its usage over the sum over all clauses.
- Pick next the candidate with the largest sum of shares over its checks outside K.
- When every unranked candidate has a sum of 0, empty K and apply the rule again.
- Candidates with empty checks go last. Final ties follow the seeded order.

1. Read CLAUSES.md and TESTLIST.md. Change neither.
2. Build candidates in the order the harness gives. Log a new candidate in ADDED.md with its checks and relies.
3. Write one failing test for the first open candidate and watch it fail.
4. Pass it with the smallest change. Refactor on green. Commit each green.

**Measure:** the usage share covered by the built candidates' checks after each iteration. Candidates logged in ADDED.md.

methodologies.title: Evaluating on a new repo

3. Run each method on its own branch from the same base commit.

spec.title: Specification
spec.text: Excerpt of the Assignment 2 brief ("Making Changes"), adapted for this experiment. The game rules and the output format are in `README.md`. Example specs are in `examples/`.

spec.title: Task
spec.text: Implement Kalah so that it supports all four variants below, and keep the implementation alterable. The variant is chosen by the two boolean parameters of `play()`.

spec.title: Restrictions
spec.text:
A significant amount of the assessment is based on an automatic marking system. If you ignore any of the following restrictions, your submission will not be marked.

- No Java 9 (or later) features, including JDK. Java 8 is allowed.
- No reference to any other files (e.g. use of configuration files).
- No use of third-party libraries.
- Do not use `System.exit()` under any circumstances.

spec.title: The play() method
spec.text:
A test suite tests all variants together through this method:

```java
    /**
     * Play a game of Kalah.
     * @param io Where to get input from and direct output to
     * @param clockwise If true, then sowing of seeds should be done in a clockwise direction,
     * otherwise if false sowing should be in an anti-clockwise direction.
     * @param sevenfive If true, then the game should have 7 houses per player, and start with 5 seeds in each house,
     * otherwise if false then it should have 6 houses per player starting with 4 seeds per house.
     */
    public void play(IO io, boolean clockwise, boolean sevenfive) {
      ....
    }
```

The `Kalah.java` stub runs the anti-clockwise 6-4 variant because of the parameters its `main()` passes to `play()`. To play another variant, change those values:

```java
  public static void main(String[] args) {
      new Kalah().play(new MockIO(), false, false); // Change values of boolean parameters as needed
  }
```

So to change to the clockwise 6-4 variant, change the first parameter to true.

spec.title: Variants
spec.text: Your implementation must allow all 4 variants: 6 houses with 4 seeds both clockwise and anti-clockwise, and 7 houses with 5 seeds both clockwise and anti-clockwise. The specific variant being tested is given by how `clockwise` and `sevenfive` are set. The test cases are the same scenarios for each variant (4 sets of test cases). `examples/EXAMPLES.md` lists a sample of the test specifications.
